result:
Thresholds are where the real music plays. We treat life as a string of destinations—the promotion, the wedding, the summit—while the actual texture unfolds in the passages between them, in those unscripted intervals where the old self dissolves but the new one has not yet arrived. I think of them constantly: the strange hour of 6:47 a.m. in a neighborhood café, just before the rush, when the espresso machine hisses its last private sigh and the barista wipes the counter in slow, circular motions, not because anyone is watching, but because ritual demands it. The light has not yet decided if it will be gold or gray.

We are allergic to in-between states. We label them as waiting, as delay, as inefficiency. A train platform at dusk, the peculiar ache of having said goodbye but not yet arrived, the breath held before pressing “send” on a message that might change everything—these are not interruptions to life; they are its architecture. Yet we edit them out when we tell our stories. We skip the flat stretches of Tuesday, the commute that neither elevates nor devastates. We believe coherence requires compression.

But the threshold is honest. It refuses to perform. In a doorway, you are neither fully inside nor outside; you are suspended, vulnerable to drafts from both rooms. That vulnerability is not a flaw—it is where change can actually enter. The caterpillar does not become a butterfly in a single gleaming moment; it dissolves in the chrysalis, a liquid stage that looks like death, a threshold so complete that it seems like failure.

So I try to linger. Not to manufacture meaning, but to allow it to accumulate like dust in a sunbeam. The next time you find yourself in a transition—waiting, traveling, hesitating—do not rush to fill the silence. Notice its temperature. It is probably the most important room you will occupy today.
